title: Baseline retest for cores/bench
Predecode and register one-hot ALU operation controls
motivation:
The bench history contains only the baseline, with no prior attempted
micro-optimizations or LESSONS.md. Its three routed critical paths all start
at ID/EX's binary ALU opcode: op[4] in seeds 1 and 3, and op[3] in seed 2.
The median seed reaches EX/MEM alu_result[22] in 7.87 ns, comprising 4.43 ns
of logic and 3.44 ns of routing, and reports 127.03 MHz. This makes ALU
control decoding and selection a concrete timing target. Removing decode
work after ID/EX could improve Fmax while preserving CoreMark cycle count.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the five-bit ALU operation field in the existing ID/EX control
bundle with 19 registered one-hot enables, one for each existing ALU
operation. Generate the enables from the decoder's existing binary
dec_alu_op before the ID/EX register. Feed them directly to the ALU and
select independently computed operation results with a balanced masked-OR
network, eliminating binary opcode comparisons from the EX stage. Do not
encode the enables back into a binary selector or build a priority chain.

This is one control-path micro-optimization: retain the existing pipeline
boundaries, instruction latencies, operand forwarding, bus handshakes,
redirect behavior, retirement width, and architectural arithmetic. Hold
the enables with their instruction during a stall and clear them on an
ID/EX flush or reset; an all-zero selector must yield zero. Keep the
decoder's default-illegal policy and all validated opcode/funct matches.
Preserve every real RV32M expression and division corner-case guard, and
apply the identical one-hot selection to the unchanged ALTOPS formulas.

The expected gain is approximately 6 percent from Fmax alone. Added
control flops, select-net routing, or a new ID-stage critical path could
offset it, so confidence is medium. Validate with existing lint, cocotb,
formal and stalled cosim gates, then compare the standard three-seed median
Fmax and marker-bracketed CoreMark fitness against 282.82. CoreMark should
retain its baseline cycle count under the same stall sequence and pass
the existing CRC and UART validation without changing any evaluation file.

implementation_notes:
Implemented the registered one-hot ALU control hypothesis. The standard repository evaluation improved fitness from 282.82 to 310.65 (+9.84%), with exactly the baseline CoreMark cycle count.

Changes:
- Replaced ctrl_t.alu_op with 19-bit alu_sel, indexed by the unchanged ALU_ADD through ALU_REMU constants. The decoder retains its binary output, default-illegal policy, and all validated opcode/funct matches.
- ID generates 19'b1 << dec_alu_op before the existing ID/EX register. Existing reset/flush priority clears the entire bundle, including every enable; existing stalls hold the complete instruction and selector.
- EX feeds the registered enables directly to the ALU. All operand muxes, forwarding, redirects, misalignment handling, PC+4 link results, pipeline boundaries, bus handshakes, and the declared nret=1 retirement interface are unchanged.
- ALU operation results are computed independently and masked by their corresponding enable. A balanced binary OR tree uses 32 leaves, with 13 constant-zero padding leaves removed by synthesis. There is no priority selection, binary re-encoding, or EX-stage binary opcode comparison. An all-zero selector yields zero.
- Preserved every original arithmetic expression, signed cast, width, shift rule, division/remainder corner-case guard, and RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS formula and constant.
- Adapted the existing ALU test driver without changing existing arithmetic vectors or expected results. Added zero-selector checks and all 361 ordered operation-enable transitions with fixed operands.
- Added two mixed-operation pipeline tests covering all 19 enables, load-use bubbles, four- and three-cycle store/load stalls, a taken redirect, and a taken branch held behind a five-cycle store stall. They check exact retirement PCs/instructions/order/results, forwarded operands, memory results, and stable bus requests. Existing tests and assertions remain intact; the harness defaults to its original zero-wait behavior.

Validation:
- Lint: PASS, no Verilator warnings, for both real arithmetic and RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS. Used the existing Makefile's core_pkg.sv-first source order; raw alphabetical glob ordering does not respect the compilation-unit typedef dependency.
- Cocotb: PASS, all five pytest runners and all 82 cocotb tests (26 ALU, 30 decoder, 8 immediate-generator, 13 pipeline, 5 register-file).
- Local formal: PASS, 53 passed / 0 failed, using the unchanged formal/run_all.sh with automatic nret=1 wrapper/config selection and JOBS=6. No RTL fix attempts or counterexamples. The first launch exited before generating checks because the default Homebrew Python lacked PyYAML; rerunning with the installed Miniconda Python completed the full gate.
- Standard cosim gate: PASS, selftest and CoreMark (2 ELFs). Additional selftest cosim with --istall --dstall matched all 115 RVFI retirements against the unchanged Python ISS.
- Yosys synthesis and all three standard nextpnr seeds: PASS. Yosys emitted its normal array-to-register-list lowering messages for the two combinational arrays; the Verilator lint gates were clean.
- git diff --check: PASS. No evaluation source, configuration, benchmark source, other core, or core.yaml was modified.

Standard repository benchmark comparison, ITERATIONS=10, -O3, --bench --istall --dstall:

| Metric | Baseline | One-hot ALU |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Seed 1 routed Fmax (MHz) | 128.72 | 139.53 |
| Seed 2 routed Fmax (MHz) | 127.03 | 137.82 |
| Seed 3 routed Fmax (MHz) | 123.02 | 139.53 |
| Median Fmax (MHz) | 127.03 | 139.53 |
| Marker-bracketed CoreMark cycles | 4,491,485 | 4,491,485 |
| Fitness | 282.82 | 310.65 |
| LUT4 | 9,563 | 9,967 |
| Flip-flops | 1,866 | 1,879 |

The improvement is entirely Fmax: +9.84%, with zero cycle-count difference under the standard deterministic stall sequence. All three routed critical paths now start at registered alu_sel[ALU_MULHU], mapped to cpu.id_ex_w[63], rather than a binary opcode bit. Seed 1 reports 3.82 ns logic + 3.35 ns routing; seed 2 3.97 + 3.29 ns; seed 3 4.17 + 3.00 ns.

Workload discrepancy: the checked-in bench/programs/Makefile currently defaults to COREMARK_SIZE=2000, and tools/eval/fpga.py validates that configuration's CRCs. The standard comparison above preserves those existing evaluation files and uses their 2 KB workload. The prompt describes a 6 KB workload instead. To verify that requirement separately without modifying evaluation files, compiled an additional scratch ELF with TOTAL_DATA_SIZE=6000, -O3 and the existing ITERATIONS=10. With --bench --istall --dstall it completed in 32,836,671 bracketed cycles (start 56,393; stop 32,893,064), produced crclist=0xd4b0, crcmatrix=0xbe52, crcstate=0x5e47, printed "Correct operation validated.", and reported no out-of-bounds access. This separate 6 KB run is not the workload used for the 282.82 baseline comparison.

Deviations and concerns: no architectural deviation. The only selection-tree implementation detail beyond the proposal is constant padding to obtain balanced five-level OR reduction. Area increased by 404 LUT4 and 13 flip-flops; registered selector routing still bounds the routed critical path. The existing ALTOPS formal gate does not prove real multiplier/divider arithmetic; formal-deep was not run, while the unchanged real expressions passed cocotb and cosim. Local results remain subject to the orchestrator's independent acceptance gates.

Validation used isolated scratch copies of the unchanged contract under $TMPDIR/alu-onehot-hyp-20260906-001-r1s0 so formal staging and benchmark builds did not write into protected worktree directories. Evidence there includes formal-selfcheck.log, cocotb.log, cosim.json, stalled-cosim.json, synthesis.log, fpga-result.json, cores/bench/generated/pnr_seed{1,2,3}/nextpnr.log, and coremark-6000-result.json. The requested notes are at the worktree root, as consumed by the orchestrator.
lesson: - 2026-09-06 hyp-20260906-001-r1s0 (regression, +9.84%): Moving ALU opcode decoding before ID/EX and selecting parallel results with a balanced masked-OR tree shortened EX logic, raising baseline Fmax from 127.03 to 139.53 MHz at unchanged CoreMark cycles for 404 extra LUT4 and 13 FFs, while registered ALU_MULHU selection remained on the critical path.

title: Move DIV and REM into a bounded multicycle execution unit
motivation:
The baseline puts signed and unsigned division and remainder in the same
combinational execute path as ordinary ALU operations. The median-seed
nextpnr report gives a 7.87 ns ID/EX-to-EX/MEM path (127.03 MHz), with
4.43 ns logic and 3.44 ns routing; synthesis maps its launch signal to
alu_op[3] and its endpoint to alu_result[22]. This establishes execute-path
pressure, although it does not by itself prove division is the limiting
operation. Removing the unrolled division network is a promising way to
shorten that path and reduce routing pressure. In the inspected CoreMark
list, matrix, state, and CRC sources, explicit division occurs in list
initialization and the matrix remainder is modulo 65536; this suggests
a small timed-region penalty, but dynamic DIV/REM frequency remains to
be measured. There are no recorded structural attempts in the target's
experiment log, and cores/bench/LESSONS.md is absent.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace only the combinational DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU execution backend with
one shared, bounded multicycle restoring divider. Register unsigned
operand magnitudes and sign/exception metadata at request acceptance;
perform eight binary restoring quotient steps per cycle for four work
cycles, using a 33-bit trial remainder; then register the selected and
sign-corrected quotient or remainder. Produce a response within six
clocks of acceptance when reset is inactive, and hold it until consumed.
Keep ordinary integer and all four multiply operations at their existing
latency. This is one structural change: time-multiplex division hardware
while keeping the normal pipeline fast. The expected benefit is higher
Fmax and lower divider area, offset by extra cycles on actual divides.

Accept a divide exactly once from a valid, legal EX instruction, only
when the older EX/MEM instruction can advance. Capture both fully
forwarded source values on that edge, including the originals required
by RVFI. Hold the PC and ID/EX while the divide is outstanding, but let
older MEM/WB work drain. After an older EX/MEM instruction advances,
insert a completely inert EX/MEM bubble during divider work: merely
holding that register would replay a store or duplicate retirement.
A real outstanding dmem transaction retains existing backpressure
priority. Transfer the completed result and saved instruction metadata
into EX/MEM once, atomically releasing ID/EX; forward that result through
the existing EX/MEM and MEM/WB paths. Preserve the response across
backpressure and cancel pending work on reset.

Preserve exact RV32M signed truncation, dividend-signed remainder,
divide-by-zero, INT_MIN/-1, and unsigned full-width behavior. Move the
existing four division ALTOPS formulas onto this same request/response
path using the original captured operands and the same completion
latency. Do not bypass the divider's stall protocol in formal builds.
Preserve nret=1, the top-level ports, decoder legality, memory masks,
strict in-order single retirement, and every existing evaluation check.
The short bound is deliberate: the unchanged liveness check requires
a successor retirement within its ten-cycle observation interval.

Validate exact arithmetic and handshake behavior in cocotb, then run
the unchanged formal and stalled cosim gates, including all canonical
CoreMark CRC and UART checks. Use real-arithmetic formal-deep for the
modified divider when available; ALTOPS alone is not arithmetic proof.
Evaluate with the existing three-seed FPGA flow and marker-bracketed
cycles. Against 4,491,485 baseline cycles, improvement requires
Fmax_new / 127.03 > cycles_new / 4491485. The predicted gain is an
estimate, not a measured result; a remaining multiplier or other path
bottleneck could erase it.

title: 64-entry bimodal prediction for direct control transfers
motivation:
The recorded history contains only baseline-bench-e113d0a at 282.82 iter/s;
LESSONS.md is absent and there are no previous predictor experiments.
Fetch currently selects PC+4 until EX redirects on every taken branch or
jump. Although comments describe five stages, IF/ID is combinational, so a
correctly predicted taken transfer can eliminate one younger-instruction
bubble. A small direction table should learn frequently taken loop branches
while limiting added storage near the core's 9563-LUT baseline. The key
tradeoff is whether fewer CoreMark cycles outweigh added fetch-path delay.

hypothesis.motivation:
The recorded history contains only baseline-bench-e113d0a at 282.82 iter/s;
LESSONS.md is absent and there are no previous predictor experiments.

jump. Although comments describe five stages, IF/ID is combinational, so a

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add one direct-control-transfer predictor: a 64-entry, PC[7:2]-indexed table
of two-bit saturating conditional-branch counters, with combinational read,
synchronous training, and reset to weakly not taken (01). Predict legal
conditional branches using the counter MSB and aligned JAL instructions as
taken. Derive each direct target from the current fetched instruction's B/J
immediate with one shared PC-relative target adder. JALR continues to resolve
in EX. Keep the lookup independent of register operands and EX feedback in
the same cycle; read/update collisions use the pre-edge counter value, with
no combinational training bypass.

In IF, predecode raw imem_data, positively validate the BRANCH funct3 set,
and require a word-aligned direct target before selecting it. Advance the
prediction only when the fetched instruction is accepted into ID/EX; a
prediction must not flush its own instruction. Carry a pred_taken bit with
the accepted instruction through if_id_t and id_ex_t, preserving it on a
hold and clearing it on reset or bubble. Since direct targets are computed
from that instruction rather than cached, EX can detect a direction mismatch
using this bit without adding a full-width predicted-target comparison.

EX remains authoritative for operands, branch outcome, target alignment,
link values, traps, and RVFI pc_next. Define actual_transfer as a legal,
aligned taken branch or jump. Request recovery only when pred_taken differs
from actual_transfer, gated by in.valid, !reset, and !stall. An aligned JALR
has pred_taken=0 and therefore still redirects. Recover to the resolved
branch/jump target for actual_transfer, or to in.pc+4 for a prediction that
should have fallen through. Correct predictions leave the younger target
instruction intact. Misaligned transfers retain existing trap and suppressed
link-write behavior and the architectural linear pc_next on the trap path.

Train the indexed counter exactly once when a valid, legal conditional
branch advances from EX into EX/MEM, excluding target-misalignment traps.
Increment toward 11 on taken and decrement toward 00 on not taken. Do not
train bubbles or repeatedly train a branch held behind dmem backpressure.
On dmem stalls, hold PC, ID/EX metadata, and EX/MEM, deferring recovery until
EX advances. On imem stalls, an advancing EX branch may still recover, with
recovery retaining priority over the IF stall. Preserve load-use bubbles
and MEM/WB forwarding retention. Counter aliasing may affect prediction
accuracy but must never change architectural execution.

The estimated improvement is 7 percent in iter/s, not a measured result.
Evaluate with the unchanged formal, unit-test, and stalled CoreMark cosim
gates, then the existing three-seed median-Fmax fitness measurement. The
principal risk is the imem-data-to-target-adder-to-PC timing path; predictor
accuracy and cycle savings must compensate for any Fmax loss. Keep the
nret=1 interface, decoder legality rules, memory contract, and all evaluation
invariants unchanged.

implementation_notes:
# Implementation: 64-entry bimodal direct-control predictor

Implemented the requested predictor in cores/bench only. The core remains RV32IM,
single retirement (nret=1), with the existing top-level bus and RVFI ports.

## Changes

- Added branch_predictor.sv: 64 two-bit counters, PC[7:2] indexing,
  combinational lookup, synchronous reset to 01, and saturating synchronous
  training. Lookup has no training bypass; coincident lookup/update sees the
  pre-edge state for the instruction accepted at that edge.
- IF positively recognizes the six legal conditional-branch funct3 values and
  JAL. A B/J immediate mux feeds one shared PC-relative target adder. Only
  word-aligned targets can be predicted. JALR is not predicted.
- Added pred_taken to if_id_t and id_ex_t. Prediction advances the PC only on
  accepted fetches and preserves the predicted instruction. Reset/recovery/
  bubbles clear the prediction; ID/EX holds it with its payload on dmem stalls.
- EX remains authoritative for branch conditions, JALR, alignment traps, link
  data, and RVFI pc_next. Recovery compares predicted direction with a legal,
  aligned actual transfer, qualified by valid, !reset, and !stall. Recovery
  chooses the resolved target or the instruction's PC+4. Correct predictions
  keep the younger instruction. Misaligned transfers trap with a linear next
  PC and suppressed link writes.
- EX trains exactly once per advancing legal conditional branch, excluding
  target-misalignment traps. Dmem stalls suppress both training and recovery;
  an advancing branch can recover despite an imem stall.
- The existing hazard-unit load-use bubbles and MEM/WB forwarding retention
  remain intact. Decoder legality and memory behavior are unchanged.

## Tests

All original pipeline assertions are retained. Its bus driver now services
stores only at accepted handshakes, supports deterministic stalls, and checks
contiguous RVFI order, exact instruction identity, and every adjacent PC link.

Added direct predictor coverage for all 64 reset entries, saturating transitions,
disabled updates, independent indices, reset priority, and old-counter collisions.
Pipeline coverage includes warm-up/exit, changing branch outcomes, opposite
directions at colliding indices, consecutive JALs, backward JAL, link forwarding,
JALR bit-zero clearing/fallback, all six legal branch conditions, load-use
dependencies, four-cycle load/store stalls, retained MEM/WB forwarding, exactly
one training event per advancing branch, both recovery directions coincident
with imem stalls, wrong-path stores/retirements, reserved BRANCH/JALR encodings,
and misaligned B/J/JALR traps with suppressed writes.

The warmed zero-wait three-instruction loop takes three cycles per iteration;
its first taken resolution adds one bubble and its exit adds one recovery.

## Local validation

- Verilator lint: PASS, no warnings. Used the repository-required compilation
  order (core_pkg.sv first) with -Wall -Wno-MULTITOP -sv and the RTL include path.
- Formal: PASS, 53 passed / 0 failed, first attempt; no RTL fixes or retries.
  Ran the unchanged bash formal/run_all.sh with CORE_NAME=bench,
  RTL_DIR=cores/bench/rtl, JOBS=4. It selected wrapper_si.sv/checks_si.cfg.
- Unit tests: PASS, all six runners and 86 cocotb checks, including 18 pipeline
  checks and the predictor-table check. The new stall test initially placed a
  poison store directly after EBREAK; since EBREAK is a retirement marker, its
  ordinary successor may reach MEM before termination. A NOP now occupies that
  slot. No existing assertion was removed and no RTL correction was needed.
- Unchanged cosim gate: PASS, selftest RVFI comparison and CoreMark with both
  --istall and --dstall (two ELFs).
- FPGA fitness: PASS, all three seeds completed normally. Ran the unchanged
  make fpga TARGET=bench NRET=1 BENCH=fpga/core_bench_si.sv gate.
  - Final routed Fmax, seeds 1/2/3: 124.19 / 137.46 / 128.44 MHz.
  - Median Fmax: 128.44 MHz.
  - Stalled CoreMark: 4,201,766 marker-bracketed cycles for 10 iterations.
  - Fitness: 305.68 iter/s, 8.08 percent above the supplied 282.82 iter/s
    baseline. This is the local fixed-gate result, not orchestrator acceptance.
  - Area: 10,851 LUT4 and 2,007 flip-flops. LUT usage is 1,288 (13.47 percent)
    above the supplied 9,563-LUT baseline and exceeds core.yaml's 10,000-LUT
    target, though all seeds fit the device.
  - Seed 1's reported critical path runs from ID/EX to EX/MEM.

## Deviations and concerns

- The predictor training connection carries the six-bit PC index rather than a
  full PC because no other PC bits are consumed by this untagged table.
- Validation ran from an isolated copy under the existing TMPDIR:
  /Users/bonetto/bonetto/auto-arch-tournament/.claude/astra-max-20260905/bench-runs/gpt-6-astra_max-rep3/.tmp/predictor-r1s2-99s0eo85
  This avoids modifying the worktree's shared formal/riscv-formal symlink and
  keeps generated files out of protected source directories. Formal, cosim,
  FPGA scripts/configs/wrappers, reference ISS, and benchmark sources were
  copied unchanged. Logs and per-check XML are retained there.
- The installed conda Python supplies cocotb/pytest/click/YAML. FPGA invocation
  explicitly selects NRET=1 and BENCH=fpga/core_bench_si.sv, matching core.yaml;
  Makefile's stand-alone cosim-build otherwise defaults to NRET=2.
- The supplied description says 6 KB and CRCs d4b0/be52/5e47, but this checkout's
  unchanged Makefile and tools/eval/fpga.py use TOTAL_DATA_SIZE=2000, -O3,
  ITERATIONS=10, and CRCs e714/1fd7/8e3a (seed e9f5, final fcaf). Validation and
  fitness use those actual fixed gates; no evaluation contract was edited.
- Counter aliasing can reduce accuracy. The new raw-imem-to-immediate/adder/PC
  path remains a timing risk, and the measured LUT increase is the principal
  area concern. The proposed 7 percent estimate is superseded by the local
  measurement above; final acceptance belongs to the orchestrator's gates.

title: Predecode two bitwise truth-table controls before execute
motivation:
The current winner, hyp-20260906-002-r1s1, reaches fitness 340.22 at
152.81 MHz after moving division out of the combinational ALU. Its
preserved nextpnr reports in
.tmp/divider-hyp-20260906-002-r1s1/cores/bench/generated/ show that the
median seed's 6.54 ns critical path starts at ID/EX alu_op[1] and ends
at EX/MEM alu_result[7]; seed 3 starts at alu_op[2] on the same result
path. Inspecting synth.json identifies OR and XOR opcode-decode terms
upstream of the operand-combining logic on that path. This is evidence
for removing bitwise-operation decoding from EX, without assuming that
the multiplier or the sequential divider is now the bottleneck.

LESSONS.md and the experiment log record one earlier micro_opt: a full
19-bit registered ALU selector improved the original baseline's Fmax by
9.84 percent, but added 404 LUT4 and left selector routing critical.
The proposed narrower predecode targets the current winner's measured
bitwise path with only two additional control bits. It preserves the
divider improvement and aims to improve fitness through Fmax alone.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the three separately selected AND/OR/XOR ALU results with one
bitwise lane controlled by two enables computed before ID/EX:

  logic_both_en   = (dec_alu_op == ALU_AND || dec_alu_op == ALU_OR)
  logic_either_en = (dec_alu_op == ALU_OR  || dec_alu_op == ALU_XOR)

Register these enables with the existing instruction control bundle.
In EX, use the forwarded ALU operands to compute the qualified result:

  logic_result = ((a & b) & {32{logic_both_en}})
               | ((a ^ b) & {32{logic_either_en}})

For each result bit this is a Boolean function of exactly four inputs:
a[i], b[i], logic_both_en and logic_either_en. The intended mapping is
one LUT4 per bit with opcode decoding before the register. AND enables
only the first term, XOR only the second, and OR both. Both enables are
zero for every other operation, making the lane contribute zero.

Retain the binary op interface for all remaining ALU operations and for
the existing divider. Have the ordinary result case produce zero for
AND/OR/XOR, then OR its result with logic_result. Do not decode those
three binary opcodes again in EX to gate the bitwise lane, and do not
re-encode its registered enables. Keep all other arithmetic expressions,
real multiply results, and RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS formulas unchanged.

This is a single control/datapath micro-optimization. Preserve pipeline
boundaries, forwarding, bus handshakes, redirects, trap checks, nret=1
ports and retirement order. Reset and flush clear both enables with
ID/EX; stalls retain them with the same instruction. The five-clock
divider request/response protocol, operand capture and bubble handling
remain unchanged. Decoder default-illegal behavior and all validated
opcode/funct matches remain authoritative.

Expect approximately five percent more fitness than 340.22, from a
shorter opcode-to-result path with unchanged instruction cycle counts.
Confidence is medium: synthesis may refactor the final OR, added enable
routing may offset the removed decoding, or the load-use/flush path
seen in seed 2 may become limiting. Inspect the mapped lane and all
three routed timing reports to test the mechanism; do not claim an
improvement from LUT count or synthesis timing alone.

Validate through the unchanged lint, cocotb, formal and stalled cosim
gates, preserving all existing assertions. Exercise bitwise operations
with forwarded operands and held/flushed controls. Use the standard
three-seed median Fmax and marker-bracketed CoreMark fitness for the
comparison against the current winner. With the same binary and stall
sequence, bracketed cycles should be identical. Retain CRC, UART and
out-of-bounds validation and leave every evaluation-contract file intact.

title: Pipeline multiplication across the existing EX and MEM stages
motivation:
The only recorded structural attempt, hyp-20260906-002-r1s1, removed
combinational division and reached 340.22 iter/s at 152.81 MHz and 5930
LUT4. Its recorded CoreMark cycles remained 4,491,485, equal to baseline.
The winning implementation still completes all four multiply operations
inside EX. Its median-seed timing report has a 6.54 ns path from
ID/EX alu_op[1] to EX/MEM alu_result[7], including 3.29 ns of routing.
This establishes remaining execute-control/result-path pressure, but
does not establish that DSP propagation itself is the critical path.
Synthesis already shares the multiply expressions into one MULT36X36;
removing supposedly independent multipliers is therefore not the thesis.
Moving multiply completion and selection into the otherwise available
MEM stage could shorten EX without stalling every multiply globally.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Retiming the multiplier across the existing EX/MEM register boundary
will improve fitness by shortening EX and allowing independent work to
continue. Implement one two-stage, fully pipelined multiplier shared by
MUL, MULH, MULHU and MULHSU: EX produces and registers partial products;
MEM combines them and selects the architectural 32-bit result for the
existing MEM/WB register. Keep the retirement boundary and nret=1.
Ordinary ALU operations, loads, stores, branches and the accepted
five-clock divider retain their present stage placement and latency.
This is one structural change to multiply execution, not a new global
execution stage or a blocking multiplier request/response machine.

Split each operand into 16-bit limbs. Zero-extend low limbs to signed
17-bit values. Extend each upper limb with its operand's sign bit only
when that operand is signed for the selected operation: both operands
for MULH, only rs1 for MULHSU, neither for MULHU or low-half MUL. Compute
four explicitly signed 17x17 products and register their complete
34-bit values with the multiply selector. In MEM, sign-extend the
registered products to 64 bits, shift cross terms by 16 and the
high/high term by 32, and sum modulo 2^64. Use carry-save reduction
followed by one final carry-propagate addition rather than serial
wide additions. Select bits 31:0 for MUL or 63:32 for the high variants.
This arrangement avoids a second, serial signed-high correction chain.
Use portable RTL with explicit widths and inspect the resulting DSP
mapping; do not assume the new partial-product arrangement saves area.

The partial-product register advances exactly with EX/MEM. Capture
fully forwarded operands only when a valid, legal multiply advances
out of EX. Hold partial products and their selector during dmem
backpressure; reset or an EX bubble clears multiply validity. Divider
work/drain and completion cycles must not launch a held instruction
again. A multiply in MEM may finish while a younger divide starts;
normal MEM/WB draining and retained forwarding data must remain intact.
Carry the multiply flag with the existing instruction/RVFI metadata
and register its final result into MEM/WB. No multiply may request a
data-memory transaction or retire independently of that bundle.

Treat a multiply destination as unavailable in EX/MEM, just like a
load destination. Extend the existing load-use interlock to multiply
producers, with its existing conservative source-comparison policy:
hold PC and insert one ID/EX bubble on an immediate dependency, subject
to the current higher-priority dmem/divider holds. Do not forward an
EX/MEM multiply placeholder or partial product. The next EX consumer
then receives the completed result from the normal MEM/WB bypass.
Preserve youngest-writer priority, x0 handling, WB-to-ID write-first
behavior and the retained MEM/WB payload during prolonged dmem stalls.
Independent multiplies can occupy EX and MEM simultaneously, sustaining
one multiply per clock when operand hazards and buses permit it.

Move the four existing multiply ALTOPS formulas and constants to the
same multiplier pipeline, preserving its advance, bubble, reset and
dependency behavior. Formal must not regain a single-cycle bypass.
Preserve the actual divider and its ALTOPS implementation unchanged.
Keep all original multiply arithmetic vectors and expected results
when migrating their driver to the new unit. Preserve decoder
default-illegal behavior, traps, aligned memory masks, top-level ports,
contiguous RVFI order and all evaluation invariants.

The predicted fitness gain is 8 percent relative to 340.22, an estimate
rather than a measured result. Immediate multiply dependencies add a
bubble; partial-product accumulation, DSP packing, or another ALU
selector path could instead cap Fmax and erase the benefit. Measure
multiply/dependency frequency if needed, then compare unchanged-gate,
same-workload marker-bracketed cycles and three-seed median Fmax.
Improvement requires Fmax_new / 152.81 > cycles_new / cycles_best;
use actual cycle counts rather than the rounded ipc_coremark field.
Run lint, complete existing cocotb tests, unchanged formal and stalled
cosim gates, and the required CoreMark CRC/UART validation. Check real
multiplication with directed/random exact-result tests and formal-deep
when feasible; ALTOPS alone is not arithmetic proof. Report area and
timing movement along with fitness, without changing the benchmark,
wrappers, source ordering, correctness checks, or other cores.

implementation_notes:
Implemented hyp-20260906-002-r2s1: pipeline multiplication across the existing EX and MEM stages.

The requested structure is implemented and the local correctness gates pass. The measured structural hypothesis regresses on the toolchain that exactly reproduces the recorded winner: 313.86 iter/s versus 340.22 iter/s (-7.75%). No changes were made to compensate by altering the workload, checking rules, divider, or retirement contract.

Changes:

- Added `cores/bench/rtl/multiplier.sv`: four explicitly signed 17x17 limb products, each captured as a complete signed 34-bit value. Low limbs have zero sign bits. Upper limbs use signed extensions for both operands of MULH and only rs1 of MULHSU; MUL and MULHU use unsigned extensions.
- MEM sign-extends each product to 64 bits, aligns the terms, performs two carry-save reductions, then one final 64-bit carry-propagate addition modulo 2^64. The registered selector chooses the low or high architectural half. There is no serial signed-high correction.
- Multiply registers advance with EX/MEM, capture forwarded operands only on a valid legal multiply launch, retain data/selector/validity during dmem holds, and clear validity on bubbles/reset. Divider drain and completion insertion advance invalid multiply entries. The existing MEM/WB bundle captures the final result and remains the sole retirement boundary.
- Added `ctrl.is_mul`, decoded only from legal multiply operations, throughout the existing metadata bundles. Generalized the conservative load-use interlock to loads or multiplies and excluded both from EX/MEM forwarding. MEM/WB bypass eligibility still retains its payload after retirement validity is cleared by a prolonged dmem stall.
- Removed multiplication and its ALTOPS formulas from the EX ALU result path. The four original ALTOPS constants/formulas now execute from registered operands in the multiplier with the same advance/hold/bubble protocol. The divider RTL, divider ALTOPS implementation, decoder, forwarding priority unit, register file, and top-level ports are unchanged; `nret` remains 1.
- Migrated every original multiply arithmetic call site and expected value to `test_multiplier.py`, including the original 300-pair random sequence and the five multiply vectors formerly used while the divider was busy. The divider response test now varies an ADD operation during work; all original divider results, latency, handshake, reset and backpressure assertions remain. Its simultaneous multiply activity is covered at pipeline level.
- Added real and ALTOPS multiplier runners, over 4,300 exact-result checks per mode, signed/unsigned and cross-limb extremes, full 64-bit product checking in real mode, consecutive operation changes, bubbles, holds, reset cancellation, and one-edge latency checks. Pipeline tests check consecutive independent launches, all consumer classes, load-to-multiply, WAW/youngest-writer priority, x0, WB-to-ID, multiply/divide overlap, delayed consumers, simultaneous bus stalls, redirects, reset, stable accepted memory transactions, exact RVFI operands/results, and contiguous single retirement.

Validation:

- Required `verilator --lint-only -Wall -Wno-MULTITOP -sv +incdir+cores/bench/rtl cores/bench/rtl/*.sv`: PASS, no warnings. The ALTOPS lint invocation also passed.
- Complete existing/expanded cocotb suite: 7 pytest runner cases, 104 cocotb cases, all PASS. This includes separate real and ALTOPS multiplier runs. Repeated successfully with the explicitly selected OSS CAD Suite.
- Unchanged `bash formal/run_all.sh` with `RTL_DIR=cores/bench/rtl`, `CORE_NAME=bench`, automatic nret=1 wrapper/config selection: PASS, 53 passed / 0 failed on the first attempt, zero RTL fix attempts. The OSS CAD Suite rerun also passed 53 / 0. No ch0 PREUNSAT or vacuous retirement acceptance.

title: Table-free static prediction for backward branches and JAL
motivation:
The current divider-based winner reaches 340.22 iter/s at 152.81 MHz with
5,930 LUT4, but still redirects in EX for every taken branch and jump.
LESSONS.md and the log entry for hyp-20260906-003-r1s2 show that direct
prediction reduced stalled CoreMark cycles from 4,491,485 to 4,201,766
(6.45 percent). That attempt ran on the original baseline: its 305.68 iter/s
improved on baseline, but did not beat the divider winner, and its 64-entry
bimodal predictor plus fetch changes added 1,288 LUT4. It does not establish
the timing of prediction combined with the current divider-based core.
A table-free predictor is a focused way to recover loop and direct-jump
bubbles while reducing the storage, lookup, and training overhead of that
earlier design. Preserving the current winner's frequency is essential.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add one static direct-control predictor to the current cores/bench RTL:
predict legal backward conditional branches taken, forward conditional
branches not taken, and aligned JAL instructions taken. Leave JALR to EX.
This backward-taken/forward-not-taken policy requires no direction table,
target cache, history, tags, counter updates, or training connections.
The hypothesis is that loop-backedge and JAL coverage can retain enough
of the prior predictor's cycle savings to improve the current winner's
CoreMark iterations/second with much less added logic.

Predecode raw imem_data in IF, positively accepting only BRANCH funct3
0, 1, 4, 5, 6, or 7 and JAL. For a branch, use instruction bit 31 as the
backward-direction test. Construct sign-extended B/J immediates and share
one full-width PC-relative target adder between these two transfer types.
Require a word-aligned target before predicting: with an aligned current
PC, B-immediate bit 1 is instruction bit 8 and J-immediate bit 1 is
instruction bit 21, so eligibility can be decided without waiting for
the target addition. Retain all upper address bits and existing modulo
32-bit PC arithmetic. Sequential fetch still selects PC+4. Derive raw
prediction independently of flush, stall, and EX recovery to avoid a
combinational hazard-feedback loop.

IF/ID is combinational in this core, so a correct prediction removes one
redirect bubble. The predicting instruction must itself enter ID/EX;
prediction is a next-PC selection, never a flush. Advance to the predicted
target only on actual fetch acceptance. Carry exactly one pred_taken bit
with the PC and instruction in if_id_t and id_ex_t. Clear it on reset or
bubbles and retain it with the held instruction. No predicted target needs
to be registered or compared in EX because B/J targets are recomputed from
the same instruction and PC, and no cached target can become stale.

EX remains authoritative for forwarded operands, the branch condition,
target calculation, alignment traps, JAL/JALR link writes, and RVFI pc_next.
Define actual_transfer as a legal, aligned taken branch or jump. Recover
only when pred_taken differs from actual_transfer for a valid instruction
that is advancing through EX. On an actual transfer, recover to its resolved
target; on an incorrectly predicted taken branch, recover to in.pc+4.
Correct predictions preserve the younger target instruction. An aligned
JALR has pred_taken=0 and retains its normal EX recovery. Misaligned
transfers keep the current trap, suppressed link write, and linear next-PC
behavior; reserved encodings keep decoder-default illegality.

Qualify recovery with valid, !reset, !stall, and no divider wait, so a branch
held behind an older stalled memory access cannot redirect repeatedly or
discard its predicted successor. Dmem stalls and divide waits retain PC
and ID/EX prediction metadata. When EX can advance, recovery must override
an imem stall; ordinary prediction must not. Preserve the existing load-use
bubble behavior, divider operand capture/drain protocol, and retained
MEM/WB forwarding data. The current hazard-unit interface can continue
consuming redirect as the qualified recovery signal.

Estimate a 5 percent fitness improvement over 340.22 iter/s, with medium
confidence; this is unmeasured. Static direction can lose accuracy on
forward-taken branches and irregular backward branches, and the remaining
imem-to-target-adder-to-PC path can still reduce Fmax. Evaluate the product
of measured iterations/cycle and the unchanged three-seed median Fmax;
fewer cycles alone do not establish a win. Use the existing formal, unit,
stalled cosim, and FPGA gates with their exact marker and CRC checks.
Keep nret=1, top-level ports, all hard invariants, and all protected files
unchanged. This proposal changes only predictor behavior and its recovery
integration, not the divider, ALU, memory system, or pipeline depth.

implementation_notes:
# Table-free static backward-branch/JAL prediction

Implemented on the current divider-based `cores/bench` core. `nret: 1`,
top-level ports, decoder defaults, divider/ALU, memory stages, forwarding,
hazard interface, pipeline depth, and protected evaluation sources are unchanged.

## Implementation

- IF positively recognizes BRANCH funct3 0/1/4/5/6/7 and JAL from raw
  `imem_data`. Backward conditional branches predict taken; forward branches
  predict not taken; aligned JAL predicts taken. JALR resolves in EX.
- B/J immediates select one full-width PC-relative target adder. Eligibility
  uses the encoded immediate bit 1 and the aligned PC without waiting for
  target addition. All upper PC bits and modulo-32-bit arithmetic are retained.
- Raw prediction is independent of reset/flush/stall/recovery. Only an
  accepted fetch advances the speculative PC. Prediction does not flush
  its own instruction. Reset and qualified EX recovery retain priority.
- Added exactly one `pred_taken` bit to each IF/ID and ID/EX bundle. It clears
  on reset/bubbles and remains part of the held ID/EX payload.
- EX compares the carried direction against a legal, aligned actual transfer.
  Recovery requires valid, no reset, no dmem stall, and no divider wait.
  Recovery selects the resolved target or the instruction's PC+4; correct
  predictions preserve the younger target instruction. RVFI always reports
  the resolved architectural next PC. Alignment traps still suppress links
  and continue linearly.

## Tests and local verification

- Required Verilator lint command: PASS, no warnings.
- Local `bash formal/run_all.sh`: PASS, **53 passed, 0 failed** with the
  unchanged single-retirement wrapper/config and ALTOPS. No RTL fix retries
  or counterexamples. The initial launch exited before generating checks
  because system Python lacked YAML; using the installed Conda environment
  resolved the dependency issue.
- Unit suites: PASS, **6 pytest runners / 96 cocotb tests**, including all
  existing decoder, arithmetic, forwarding, divider, and pipeline checks.
- Added eight pipeline tests using the existing unchanged ISS/comparator:
  zero-bubble taken loop iterations and JAL chains; loop-exit and forward
  branch recovery; all six conditions in both directions and outcomes;
  JAL/JALR links; load-use forwarding; retained MEM/WB forwarding while a
  predicted branch/successor waits behind six dmem stall cycles; DIV/REM
  consumers; imem stalls during correct predictions and both recovery
  directions; reserved and misaligned B/J/JALR encodings.
- The handshake-aware harness additionally verifies whole-ID/EX holds,
  bubble clearing, PC holds, recovery priority, contiguous retirement order,
  exact instruction/PC chaining, and one accepted memory transaction per
  memory retirement. Wrong-path retirements and stores remain forbidden.
- Added `test_if_stage.py` for positive predecode, reset/flush/acceptance,
  recovery priority, extreme B/J offsets, full-width carries/borrows, and
  wraparound. This is the only added RTL/test file beyond the advisory list.
- Standard cosim gate: PASS, selftest plus stalled CoreMark CRC validation.
- Additional selftest with `--istall --dstall`: PASS, all **115 retirements**
  matched the unchanged RVFI comparator.

Formal and FPGA/cosim work products were staged under
`$TMPDIR/btfnt-verify.78bAzO` using unchanged copies of contract sources.
No formal, benchmark, FPGA, cosim-contract, or other-core source was edited.

## Benchmark contract discrepancy and supplemental 6 KB check

The checked-in Makefile/evaluator actually use `TOTAL_DATA_SIZE=2000`, `-O3`,
10 iterations, and exact CRCs `e9f5/e714/1fd7/8e3a/fcaf`. Those defaults and
checks were left intact for the normal cosim/FPGA gates.

The prompt also requests the 6 KB CRC set. A separate scratch build using
the unchanged benchmark Makefile with `COREMARK_SIZE=6000 COREMARK_OPT=-O3`
passed with `--bench --istall --dstall`: EBREAK reached, no OOB, literal
`Correct operation validated.`, 10 iterations, seedcrc `8a02`, crclist
`d4b0`, crcmatrix `be52`, crcstate `5e47`, crcfinal `5949`. Start/stop markers
were **54,040 / 31,140,315**, giving **31,086,275 bracketed cycles**.
This supplemental workload is not substituted into the unchanged fitness gate.

## FPGA fitness and concerns

The unchanged local FPGA gate passed all three routing seeds and its exact
CoreMark CRC, completion, OOB, and start/stop-marker checks:

- Seed 1 / 2 / 3 final Fmax: **181.36 / 182.88 / 171.26 MHz**.
- Median Fmax: **181.36 MHz**.
- Stalled CoreMark: **10 iterations / 4,259,699 bracketed cycles**.
- Fitness: `181.36e6 * (10 / 4,259,699)` = **425.76 iterations/second**,
  **25.14% above** the supplied divider winner's 340.22 iterations/second.
- Resources: **5,990 LUT4**, **2,189 FF**; LUT4 increased by **60** relative
  to the supplied 5,930-LUT4 winner.

These are local measurements using the checked-in default workload, not an
orchestrator acceptance decision. No evaluation checks or seed choices were
changed. Static direction can still mispredict forward-taken or irregular
backward branches on other workloads, and the added instruction-to-target-to-PC
path remains a timing concern beyond this measured implementation.

Evidence in the scratch directory: `formal-console.log`, `units.log`,
`cosim.log`, `stalled-selftest.json`, `sixk-result.json`, `fpga.log`, and
`cores/bench/generated/pnr_seed{1,2,3}/nextpnr.log`.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace only the two combinational register-file read networks with
explicit one-hot word selection and a balanced masked-OR reduction.
Retain the existing flop storage, synchronous reset, synchronous write
behavior, module ports, and zero-cycle read latency. Each read-address
decoder is shared across its port's 32 data bits.

For each read port p, compute:

  wb_hit_p = w_en && (rs_p_addr != 0) && (w_addr == rs_p_addr)
  stored_sel_p[i] = (rs_p_addr == i) && !wb_hit_p, for i = 1..31

Form 32 candidate words: candidate 0 is w_data masked by wb_hit_p;
candidates 1..31 are regs[i] masked by stored_sel_p[i]. Register x0
contributes no stored candidate. With an x0 read, every mask is zero.
With a same-cycle nonzero write/read collision, only the write-data
candidate contributes, so stale register contents cannot be ORed into
the bypassed value. When w_en is low, matching w_addr must not suppress
the stored value. Preserve the current combinational behavior during
reset as well as reset's priority at the write edge.

Express the reduction with static generate indices and explicit levels:
first OR adjacent pairs of masked candidates into 16 words, then OR
groups of four into four words, then OR those four into the read output.
Per data bit, each first-level pair is a four-input Boolean function
of two data bits and their two enables. The following levels are
four-input ORs. This targets three LUT4 levels from a stored data bit
to the read output, subject to actual synthesis mapping. Fold the
write-first candidate into this same tree instead of placing another
32-bit bypass mux after the register selection. Do not build a serial
OR accumulator, priority chain, variable-index read mux, or binary
re-encoder. Use explicit widths and Yosys-compatible constructs.

This is one register-file selection micro-optimization. Keep the
instruction pipeline, ALU and divider, static prediction, hazard logic,
EX/MEM and MEM/WB forwarding, bus handshakes, nret=1 ports, retirement
ordering, and all trap and decoder rules unchanged. No additional
operand register, issue bubble, or dependency latency is introduced.

Estimate six percent more fitness through Fmax alone, with medium
confidence. The estimate is unmeasured. Shared select-net fanout,
address-decode timing, bypass-hit routing, synthesis refactoring, or
another pipeline path may limit the benefit. Inspect the mapped read
network and all three routed paths; do not assume the intended LUT
depth guarantees a routed improvement. Compare LUT4/FF use and the
standard three-seed median Fmax against the 5990-LUT4, 2189-FF winner.

# One-hot register-file reads with folded write-first bypass

Implemented the requested read topology. All correctness gates pass locally,
but the measured FPGA fitness is **289.53**, versus **425.76** for the supplied
winner (**32.00% regression**). The proposed Fmax improvement is not supported
by this implementation's measurements.

## Changes

- Changed only `cores/bench/rtl/reg_file.sv` in RTL. The module interface,
  register array, and entire synchronous write/reset block are unchanged.
- Each port computes a nonzero-address write hit and shares 31 stored-word
  selects across its 32 data bits. A hit disables every stored candidate.
  Candidate 0 contains masked write data; candidates 1 through 31 contain
  masked register data. Stored x0 does not participate.

title: Replace the flop register file with replicated distributed RAM
motivation:
The current winner reaches 425.76 iterations/s at 181.36 MHz. The two
earlier structural attempts show that removing combinational division
helped, whereas pipelining multiplication lost frequency and added
dependency cycles. The retained timing reports for the winning static
predictor run now identify a different bottleneck: all three seeds
start their critical path in u_rf.regs and end in the ID/EX register.
The median seed reports 5.51 ns, comprising 3.05 ns logic and 2.47 ns
routing, from register x30 bit 16 into ID/EX. These reports are under
.tmp/btfnt-verify.78bAzO/cores/bench/generated/pnr_seed*/nextpnr.log;
their final frequencies match the logged 181.36/182.88/171.26 MHz.
The current register file resets its entire data array, forcing a
flop-based implementation with two wide asynchronous read muxes.
The installed Yosys Gowin mapping supports synchronous-write,
asynchronous-read distributed RAM through RAM16SDP primitives, and
the unchanged synth_gowin invocation does not disable LUT RAM.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace only the register-file storage architecture with two coherent
distributed-RAM replicas, one for each asynchronous read port. Broadcast
the existing single write port to both replicas. Implement each replica
as two 16x32 banks, selecting the bank with address bit 4 and indexing
it with bits 3:0. Use portable inferred memories and the distributed
RAM style attribute supported by the installed synthesis flow. The
resulting four banks should map to Gowin RAM16SDP cells, eliminating
the large flop-to-read-mux networks without adding a pipeline stage,
changing register-read latency, or introducing instruction stalls.
This is a single structural hypothesis about register-file storage
and read-port replication; the existing execution units and predictor
remain the reference configuration.

Remove reset assignments from the RAM data arrays. Instead, maintain
one shared, synchronously reset written-valid bit for each nonzero
architectural register. Reset clears every valid bit in one edge;
an accepted write sets the destination bit and writes identical data
to the addressed bank in both replicas. Gate stored writes with
!reset, w_en, and w_addr != 0, preserving reset's sequential priority.
This retains the existing observable all-registers-zero reset behavior
even after a warm reset, without relying on RAM initialization values
or a multi-cycle clearing sweep. Stale or uninitialized RAM contents
must never reach an observable read while its valid bit is clear.

Preserve the exact asynchronous read priority independently on both
ports: x0 returns zero; a matching same-cycle write returns w_data;
otherwise an invalid register returns zero, and a valid register
returns its selected RAM-bank word. Keep the current combinational
write-first bypass condition and timing, including its priority over
the stored value. Suppress all stored writes to x0. A write to a
previously invalid register must bypass correctly before the edge
and be available through both replicas after the edge. Reads of
different addresses must remain independent during writes. Reset
invalidates both replicas through the shared metadata atomically.

Preserve the reg_file interface, existing ID/EX enables, forwarding
priorities, load-use interlock, divider operand capture, retained
MEM/WB forwarding during dmem stalls, and single-channel retirement.
No register-file output is registered or delayed. There are no new
pipeline bubbles, initialization waits, or changes to formal ALTOPS.
All decoder legality, traps, memory masks, top-level ports, nret=1,
and contiguous RVFI order remain as required by the existing contract.

The expected gain is 8 percent over the current 425.76 iterations/s,
with unchanged cycle counts on the same workload and stall sequence.
This is an estimate, not a measurement. RAM-bank selection, valid-bit
lookup, WB bypass, or the existing EX path could become the new timing
limit; distributed-memory placement and write fanout could erase the
benefit. Inspect synthesized RAM16SDP counts, remaining register-file
data flops, LUT4/FF totals, and all three routed timing reports to
verify the proposed storage structure actually survives synthesis.

Run the complete existing unit, formal, and stalled cosim gates, with
additional register-file reset/coherency and pipeline dependency tests.

preserve the required 6 KB CRCs d4b0/be52/5e47, validated UART literal,
bounded addresses, and start/stop markers. Only cores/bench RTL and
its allowed unit tests are implementation targets.

title: Four-entry return stack for JALR prediction
motivation:
The recorded winner, hyp-20260906-003-r2s2, reaches 425.76 iter/s with
181.36 MHz median Fmax, 5,990 LUT4, and 4,259,699 bracketed cycles. Its
static backward-branch/JAL predictor added only 60 LUT4, but every JALR,
including a function return, still requires EX recovery. Correctly
predicting a return can preserve its younger successor and remove the
one recovery bubble in this core's combinational IF/ID organization.

LESSONS.md and the predictor entries in experiments/log.jsonl show that
hyp-20260906-003-r1s2 added 1,288 LUT4 with a 64-entry bimodal predictor
and fetch changes. That attempt used an earlier base, so its timing is
not a measurement on today's divider-based winner. A small return stack
targets an uncovered control-transfer class while retaining the current
direct predictor. Return frequency and achievable frequency are not yet
measured for this proposal; the expected gain is a hypothesis.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add exactly one predictor mechanism: a four-entry return-address stack
(RAS), updated only by advancing EX instructions, with fetch prediction
restricted to canonical returns. Keep the current backward-taken branch
policy, aligned JAL prediction, shared B/J target adder, divider, pipeline
depth, and hazard behavior. This proposal adds no conditional-direction
table or general indirect-target cache.

Implement four full-width 32-bit address registers as a fixed-position
shift stack with entry zero always holding the newest return address.
Fetch reads that register directly, avoiding an indexed target-read mux.
Use a three-bit occupancy count in the range zero through four. Reset
clears occupancy and entries. Push shifts toward the oldest entry and
inserts the resolving instruction's full modulo-32-bit PC+4; when full,
discard the oldest entry and retain occupancy four. A nonempty pop shifts
toward entry zero, zeroes the vacated entry, and decrements occupancy.
Empty pop is a no-op. Simultaneous pop then push replaces the top when
nonempty, or performs a normal push when empty. These bounded policies
must not wrap the count or expose discarded entries as valid predictions.

Follow the RISC-V x1/x5 call/return hints for EX updates. A legal aligned
JAL pushes only if rd is x1 or x5. For a legal aligned JALR: push when rd
is a link register and rs1 is not; pop when rs1 is a link register and rd
is not; push only when rd and rs1 are the same link register; pop then
push when both are link registers but differ; otherwise do neither.
Hint reference: https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/v20260120/unpriv/rv32.html

Qualify every stack action with in.valid, !reset, !stall, !div_wait,
legal decoded jump control, and absence of target-misalignment fault,
exactly when that instruction advances into EX/MEM. Never update from
IF acceptance or from a flushed instruction. An advancing call/return
must perform its action even when it also asserts recovery. A held EX
instruction performs no action until it advances, then acts once.
This ordering avoids speculative stack checkpoints and rollback state:
a younger wrong-path instruction is killed before it can update in EX.

In IF, positively recognize raw imem_data as JALR with funct3=000, rd=x0,
rs1=x1 or x5, and immediate zero. Predict such a return taken only when
the current PC and nonempty stack top are word aligned. Select the full
stored address directly as the predicted next PC. Empty-stack returns
and all other JALRs retain the current sequential-fetch/EX-recovery
fallback. Raw return recognition and the stack read must not depend on
flush, stall, redirect, forwarded operands, or same-cycle EX update data.
Do not bypass an EX push/pop into fetch: simultaneous lookup and update
deliberately use the pre-edge top. This can miss a call whose first
target instruction is a return, or consecutive returns, but saves an
EX-to-IF bypass path and is corrected by ordinary target recovery.

Retain pred_taken and add a 32-bit pred_target to if_id_t and id_ex_t.
Set pred_target to the selected stack address for a predicted return
and zero otherwise. Both prediction fields belong to the accepted PC
and instruction: hold them with ID/EX on dmem/divider stalls and clear
them on reset and bubbles. Change the PC through prediction only when
the instruction actually enters ID/EX; never flush the predicting
instruction. Existing reset and qualified EX recovery priority remain.

EX must resolve JALR from the fully forwarded rs1 plus immediate, clear
target bit zero, and retain all current alignment, trap, link-write,
and actual RVFI pc_next behavior. The current direction-only recovery
is insufficient for a RAS: both prediction and execution can be taken
with different targets. With the existing advance qualification, recover
when pred_taken differs from actual_transfer, OR when pred_taken and
actual_transfer are both true for JALR and the saved full pred_target
differs from jump_target. Direct B/J predictions keep their existing
direction-only comparison. A stale top, modified link register, stack
overflow, or different calling convention must affect performance only.
Correct returns preserve the successor; wrong targets recover to the
actual jump target; a predicted return that traps recovers to PC+4 with
the existing trap and suppressed-link semantics. RVFI never reports a
speculative target as the architectural next PC.

Preserve recovery overriding imem backpressure when EX can advance,
deferred recovery and updates during dmem/divider holds, load-use
bubbles, and retained MEM/WB forwarding. Add focused unit and pipeline

title: Retime write-through register-file bypass into EX forwarding
motivation:
The retained winner reaches 425.76 fitness at 181.36 MHz median Fmax.
Its preserved routed reports in .tmp/btfnt-verify.78bAzO show register-file
storage-to-ID/EX read paths limiting all three seeds at 5.51, 5.47 and
5.84 ns. The current read path selects a stored word, applies same-cycle
WB write-through, and captures the resulting operand in ID/EX.

LESSONS.md and experiments/log.jsonl warn against broad read-network
changes: hyp-20260906-001-r3s0 flattened the register-file muxes but lost
32 percent fitness when unchanged EX logic became critical. The RAM
alternative lost 16.70 percent. Earlier ALU predecode attempts also left
control routing critical. This proposal targets only the location of
WB write-through selection, retaining the current storage and indexed
read topology and preserving every instruction's execution latency.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Move same-cycle WB-to-ID operand bypass selection across the existing
ID/EX boundary and absorb it into EX's existing forwarding selection.
Register raw register-file operands in the current rs1_val/rs2_val
fields. Alongside them, capture one shared 32-bit WB data snapshot and
two source-hit flags. Each flag is computed in ID from the actual
valid-qualified WB write enable, a nonzero WB destination, and equality
with that source address. Both operands can use the same snapshot
because the core has one WB write port. This adds 34 ID/EX bits and
no new pipeline stage or instruction cycle.

Add a compile-time WRITE_THROUGH parameter to reg_file, defaulting to
one so its existing standalone contract and tests remain unchanged.
Set it to zero only for the core's register-file instance. In that
configuration, reads select the existing regs[address] with the same
x0 override, without the WB-data bypass mux. Keep the storage array,
synchronous write/reset process, all-register reset and nonzero-write
rule intact. Do not replace the indexed reads, infer a different memory
primitive, or change storage layout as part of this hypothesis.

ID receives WB enable, address and data directly from the existing WB
wires. Capture raw operands, the common WB data and both hit flags on
exactly the same existing ID/EX advance. Reset or flush clears the full
payload, including all added fields; an ID stall holds it all. Snapshot
data may be captured unconditionally on an advance because the flags
qualify its use. Never reconstruct a missed WB value from the next
cycle's live WB bus: that producer may already have disappeared.

For each EX operand, retain this exact priority: current EX/MEM forward,
current MEM/WB forward, captured ID-time WB snapshot when its hit flag
is set, then captured raw register-file data. A newer producer must
override an older snapshot. Form four mutually exclusive qualifiers
using the current forwarding selections and the registered hit flag,
and combine the four masked words with a balanced pairwise OR. Fold
the snapshot into this single selection network; do not put a separate
snapshot-versus-raw mux in series ahead of the old forwarding mux.
The existing forward_unit comparisons and EX/MEM-over-MEM/WB priority
can remain unchanged. No binary ALU-op recoding is part of this change.

Use the resulting rs1/rs2 for every current EX consumer: ALU operands,
branch comparison, JALR address, store data and original RVFI operands.
Division must capture these fully resolved sources and RVFI metadata
on its existing request edge. Preserve the five-clock divider protocol,
retained MEM/WB forwarding during dmem stalls, and all existing bubble,
redirect, prediction, alignment-trap and retirement behavior. Keep real
RV32M arithmetic and RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS expressions unchanged. The core
remains nret=1 with identical external ports and legality checks.

The timing hypothesis is that removing WB selection from the critical
stored-word-to-ID/EX path outweighs the cost of a fourth EX forwarding
candidate. Expect four percent higher fitness from Fmax alone, with
low confidence: the rejected register-file attempts show that mapping
can expose a much slower EX path, and the new snapshot bus adds routing
and flops. Inspect mapped and routed paths in both stages; a shorter
register-file path alone is insufficient evidence of improvement.

Validate the new raw-read configuration and exact bypass priority with
directed unit/pipeline tests, retaining all existing assertions. Run
the unchanged lint, formal, cosim and three-seed FPGA gates. Compare
marker-bracketed cycles using identical before/after ELFs and bus-stall
sequences; cycle counts should be identical. Use the logged fitness
workload consistently for the 425.76 comparison, and retain the
requested 6 KB CRC, UART, bounds and marker validation. Change no
benchmark sources, evaluation settings or correctness contracts.

implementation_notes:
# Retimed register-file write-through bypass

Implemented the hypothesis without changing instruction latency or pipeline
control. All local correctness gates pass. The measured FPGA fitness is
**351.22**, versus the retained winner's **425.76**: a **17.51% regression**.
The proposed performance gain is not supported by these measurements.

## Implementation

- Added default-enabled `reg_file.WRITE_THROUGH`. Only the core instance
  disables it. Both read ports retain indexed `regs[address]` reads and the
  x0 override. The storage declaration and complete synchronous write/reset
  block are unchanged, including all-register reset and nonzero writes.
- Added exactly 34 bits to `id_ex_t`: one 32-bit `wb_snapshot` and the two
  `rs1_wb_hit` / `rs2_wb_hit` flags. Raw operands remain in `rs1_val` and
  `rs2_val`; downstream bundles and `ctrl_t` are unchanged.
- ID receives the existing WB write wires. Each flag requires the actual
  valid-qualified write enable, a nonzero destination, and its source-address
  match. Raw data, snapshot, and flags advance together on the existing edge,
  hold during ID stalls, and clear with the entire payload on reset/flush.
- Each EX operand uses four mutually exclusive masks and a balanced pairwise
  OR: current EX/MEM, current MEM/WB, captured WB snapshot, then captured raw
  data. There is no separate snapshot/raw mux ahead of forwarding. Existing
  forwarding comparisons and retained MEM/WB behavior are unchanged.
- The existing resolved `rs1` / `rs2` signals still feed ALU inputs, branches,
  JALR, stores, and RVFI originals. Division's existing request edge captures
  these resolved values and retirement metadata. Divider state, five-clock
  response protocol, real arithmetic, and ALTOPS expressions are unchanged.
- Top-level ports, `nret: 1`, prediction, alignment traps, legality, retirement,
  hazard behavior, and all protected evaluation sources are unchanged.

There are no architectural deviations from the proposed change. Validation
ran in an isolated scratch copy because the worktree's formal-framework
symlink is shared. No evaluation-contract file or other core was edited.

## Tests and local gates

- Required Verilator lint command and unchanged `make lint TARGET=bench`:
  **PASS**, without warnings or errors.
- Unchanged `bash formal/run_all.sh`, with `RTL_DIR=cores/bench/rtl` and
  `CORE_NAME=bench`: **PASS, 53 passed / 0 failed**, first attempt. Automatic
  nret detection selected the original single-retirement wrapper/config.
  No counterexample, RTL correction, or formal retry was needed.
- Unchanged `make test TARGET=bench`: **PASS, 7 pytest runners / 101 cocotb
  tests**: 28 ALU, 30 decoder, 2 IF, 8 immediate, 27 pipeline, 5 original
  register-file tests, and 1 new raw-read scoreboard test.
- The new raw-read runner sets `WRITE_THROUGH=0`; the existing default-mode
  tests remain unchanged. The scoreboard checks all 1,024 read-address pairs,
  every nonzero register on either/both collision ports, old/new values before
  and after the edge, consecutive and disabled writes, x0, and reset priority.
- Four added pipeline tests contain 88 directed programs. They exercise ALU
  and load WB/ID collisions on either/both sources; snapshot-only execution
  with neither forwarding stage matching and a different live WB value;
  newer EX/MEM and MEM/WB writers, including repeated writes; arithmetic,
  branches, JALR, store address/data, and all DIV/REM variants; x0; imem
  backpressure; and snapshot holds behind stalled memory and division.
- The existing handshake-aware harness now also checks raw RF reads against
  an independent storage scoreboard, valid-qualified ID hit capture, original
  write-through equivalence, the exact EX selection priority, full-payload
  hold/clear, and division's accepted operands/metadata throughout its wait.
  Its original ISS comparison, PC chaining, order, load-use/redirect checks,
  and one accepted bus transaction per memory retirement remain intact.
- Existing timing assertions are retained. Added checks confirm ordinary
  collision consumers retire on the same cycle and division keeps its
  established protocol. An initial new assertion counted from the pre-edge
  request sample instead of the acceptance edge; that test-only off-by-one
  was corrected. No RTL change was required. All existing assertions passed.
- Unchanged `make cosim TARGET=bench`, with `NRET=1`: **PASS**, selftest and
  stalled CoreMark validation. Additional selftest with `--istall --dstall`:
  **PASS**, all 115 retirements matched the unchanged RVFI comparator.
- Unchanged `make fpga TARGET=bench`, with `NRET=1` and the single-retirement
  FPGA wrapper selected through `BENCH`: all three seeds routed, and the
  unchanged workload/CRC/marker/bounds validation passed.

## Identical workloads and cycle comparison

The checked-in fitness gate defaults to 2 KB, -O3, ITERATIONS=10 and the 2 KB
CRC set. That is the workload behind 425.76; it was preserved. The requested
6 KB CRC workload was validated separately. Both retained ELFs were reused
byte for byte, with no benchmark-source or evaluation-setting change.

The original RTL was copied before editing and built into its own simulator.
Both simulators ran each identical ELF with `--bench --istall --dstall` and
the unchanged harness's default deterministic bus-stall seed. The complete
before/after completion-marker JSON, including UART and markers, is identical.

| Workload | Start marker | Stop marker | Bracketed cycles, before and after |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Logged 2 KB fitness workload | 15,189 | 4,274,888 | 4,259,699 |
| Required 6 KB validation | 54,040 | 31,140,315 | 31,086,275 |

Both runs reached EBREAK, reported no out-of-bounds access, contained
`Correct operation validated.`, completed 10 iterations, and had valid
start/stop markers. The standard run passed `validate_coremark_uart`
unchanged. The 6 KB run matched seedcrc=8a02, crclist=d4b0, crcmatrix=be52,
crcstate=5e47, and crcfinal=5949.

ELF SHA-256 values:

- Standard: `c2af1db144cd8fc7936f33f0a0e05a244938ebfc64c5fd362e5ffe88cde4a0d4`
- 6 KB: `34fc0213570a1ca40d9180265d08d29195619518e9645b1c04d1ebe42d2b0f00`

## FPGA results and timing concerns

| Metric | Retained winner | Retimed bypass |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Seed 1 Fmax, MHz | 181.36 | 133.33 |
| Seed 2 Fmax, MHz | 182.88 | 149.61 |
| Seed 3 Fmax, MHz | 171.26 | 153.05 |
| Median Fmax, MHz | 181.36 | 149.61 |
| LUT4 utilization | 5,990 | 6,039 |
| FF utilization | 2,189 | 2,223 |
| Fitness, iterations/second | 425.76 | 351.22 |

Fitness uses `149.61e6 * (10 / 4,259,699)`, not the evaluator's rounded IPC
display. Area increases by 49 LUT4 and exactly the proposed 34 FFs. Both
mapped netlists retain 992 register-file DFFE storage cells; no RAM primitive
or alternate storage implementation was introduced.

A structural walk of the mapped combinational primitives to each ID/EX raw
operand D input shows port 1's maximum depth per bit falling from six cells
to five. Port 2 changes from six cells on 6 bits / seven on 26 bits to five
on 9 bits / six on 22 bits / seven on 1 bit. These counts include mapped
mux primitives and are structural depths, not routed delays.

The corresponding maximum mapped paths into EX/MEM's resolved operand
registers grew on both ports: ID/EX-origin paths from six to eight cells,
and EX/MEM-origin forwarding paths from seven to nine cells. These include
the existing final EX register selection and show a cost beyond raw RF reads.

All three final critical routed paths were inspected and endpoints resolved
against the packed-bundle aliases in `synth.json`:

| Seed | Source | Endpoint | Total ns | Logic ns | Routing ns |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | ID/EX alu_op[1] | EX/MEM alu_result[1] | 7.50 | 2.99 | 4.51 |
| 2 | ID/EX alu_op[2] | EX/MEM alu_result[1] | 6.68 | 3.10 | 3.58 |
| 3 | EX/MEM rd[2], also instr[9] | EX/MEM rs1_val[20] | 6.53 | 3.13 | 3.41 |

Totals use Fmax; independently rounded logic/routing columns can differ by
0.01 ns. The retained winner's critical paths are RF storage to ID/EX rs2
at 5.51 / 5.47 / 5.84 ns. This implementation moves the bottleneck into EX,
including forwarding control in seed 3, and reduces overall Fmax.

A supplemental seed-1 route with report-output options reproduced the same
133.33 MHz critical path. Its detailed net timing report was also inspected
at ID/EX raw-data and hit-flag endpoints, alongside EX endpoints. It lists
all 32 raw-rs1 D arrivals and both hit-flag arrivals, but only a subset of
raw-rs2 endpoints and no snapshot-data endpoint entries; it is not treated
as a complete independent timing bound for those omitted paths. A preliminary
attempt to reload the packed/routed JSON for reporting hit a nextpnr internal
assertion, so the detailed report was obtained by repeating seed 1 with the
same placement/routing settings. The original three-seed gate result stands.

Removing write-through selection does shorten some mapped RF paths, but the
fourth forwarding candidate and changed mapping/routing outweigh that benefit.
No broader ALU or forwarding redesign was attempted to rescue this hypothesis.
These are local measurements, not an orchestrator acceptance decision.

Evidence is retained in:
`$TMPDIR/wb-retime-verify.e1pv_w52/`

Key artifacts: `formal-gate.log`, `lint-gate.log`, `unit-gate-final.log`,
`cosim-gate.log`, `stalled-selftest.json`, `cycle-comparison.json`,

`routed-detail-seed1.json`, and

title: Decouple instruction fetch with a two-entry fall-through queue
motivation:
The retained winner reaches 425.76 iter/s at 181.36 MHz, with 5,990
LUT4 and 4,259,699 marker-bracketed cycles in the recorded fitness run.
Its combinational IF/ID interface ties fetch advancement to decode
acceptance: load-use bubbles, dmem backpressure and divider waits all
hold the fetch PC, even when imemReady is high. Conversely, imemReady
low immediately removes the instruction offered to decode. A small
queue can use otherwise idle fetch opportunities during backend holds
and spend those buffered instructions during later instruction stalls.

LESSONS.md and the structural entries in experiments/log.jsonl show
that the bounded divider improved fitness, whereas multiply retiming
lost 7.75 percent and distributed-RAM register storage lost 16.70
percent. Those regressions retained an EX control/result timing limit;
area savings or another functional-unit pipeline are not sufficient
evidence of a speedup. No recorded structural attempt decouples fetch
from decode. This proposal targets lost overlap under the specified
approximately 22 percent bus stalls; its dynamic benefit is unmeasured.
